samples.brief: framework fw:nested_loops for topic: a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C brands; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Open the outer story > Open the middle story > Deliver the core > Close inner to outer), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
[Open the outer story] March last year, 11 pm, my phone buzzes. It's the founder of a block-print brand we file for. "Sir, GST notice aaya hai. Reply kab tak?" She'd found it on the portal three weeks late. Most of the reply window was gone.

[Open the middle story] I'd been there once, as an article assistant in a C-Scheme office. My principal handed me an ASMT-10 for a textile trader and said, "Tum dekh lo." I assumed it was routine and left it for ten days. The mismatch was real, and the deadline was close.

[Deliver the core] Both nights taught me one thing. A GST notice is rarely lost on the law. It is lost on the calendar. Most D2C mismatches have a paper answer: a marketplace TCS figure, a supplier who filed late, a credit note nobody matched. Collecting that paper takes days. So our rule is boring on purpose: we check every client's portal every week, and every notice gets a reply date on our board the day it lands.

[Close inner to outer] That ASMT-10? We pulled the supplier invoices over a weekend and filed a day before the deadline. Nothing was owed, but it was too close. I haven't let a notice sit since. And the block-print founder? We filed her reply, marketplace statements attached, inside the window. This time the calendar was ours. She now forwards every portal email within the hour, and we still check her portal weekly.

samples.brief: framework fw:nut_graf_feature for topic: a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Lede > Nut graf > Body > Kicker), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
[Lede] At 11:50 on a Tuesday, the Kharadi kitchen of ProtiThali smells of roasted soya and hing. A cook weighs paneer for each box on a steel scale before it goes into the gravy; nobody eyeballs it. At noon, the first orders from the IT parks start pinging.

[Nut graf] For most of Pune's office workers, lunch has meant rice, thin dal and a slow afternoon. A growing group of eaters, gym regulars and people managing blood sugar among them, now checks protein before price. This week ProtiThali launches a high-protein thali for them. This story asks whether a delivery kitchen can hit a protein number every day, at a thali price, without the food tasting like a diet plan.

[Body] What is in the box: paneer, soya chunks, sprouted moong and a dal cooked thick, with protein per thali at [lab-tested figure, to confirm with report]. Why now: [founder quote on what customers kept asking for]. Is it enough: [named Pune dietitian on who this suits and who it does not]. The other side: rival kitchens say protein menus cost more to make and come back half-eaten; the thali sells at [₹ price] against [₹ price] for the regular one, and that gap is the bet.

[Kicker] At 12:05 the first rider leaves for Hinjewadi with six boxes. On the whiteboard, someone rubs out "dal fry" and writes "dal, thick". By month-end, repeat orders will say whether Pune wanted this or only said it did.

samples.brief: framework fw:oath for topic: an AI tool that turns Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Oblivious > Apathetic > Thinking > Hurting), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
BoloMinutes turns Hindi and Hinglish voice notes into meeting minutes. Four openings, one for each reader state.

[Oblivious] Tuesday ki site meeting mein tay hua tha ki cement Friday tak aayega. Friday aaya, cement nahi aaya. Teen logon ne woh 6 minute ka voice note dobara suna, aur teeno ko alag baat yaad thi. Aapki team ke decisions bhi shayad kisi voice note mein band hain, jo koi dobara nahi sunta.

[Apathetic] "Chalta hai, sab ko yaad rehta hai." Rehta hai, jab tak koi galat yaad nahi rakhta. Phir wahi kaam do baar hota hai, vendor ko do alag date bata di jaati hai, aur Saturday ka aadha din yeh dhoondhne mein jaata hai ki kisne kya kaha tha.

[Thinking] Teen raaste hain. Ek, kisi junior se notes likhwao: Hindi samajhta hai, par har meeting mein nahi hota. Do, English transcription app: Hinglish mein aadhe shabd ulte likh deta hai. Teen, BoloMinutes: voice note sunke decisions, kaam kiska hai aur date kya hai, teeno alag likhta hai, Hindi ya English mein. [accuracy on a sample of your own notes, from our test]. Data ka sawal? [storage and deletion policy, to confirm with legal].

[Hurting] Kal subah client ko minutes bhejne hain? Voice note hamare WhatsApp number pe forward kijiye, minutes PDF mein wapas aayenge. Pehle 10 notes free, card nahi chahiye.

samples.brief: framework fw:oreo for topic: a government scheme that gives rooftop-solar subsidies to households; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Opinion > Reason > Explanation / Example > Opinion), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
[Opinion] If you own your house and your roof gets sun from morning to late afternoon, apply for the rooftop-solar subsidy this year, not "when the bill gets worse".

[Reason] The subsidy takes the biggest bite out of the one number that stops most families: the upfront cost. You pay a registered vendor, the discom inspects and fits a net meter, and the subsidy is credited to your bank account. After that, whatever your panels make during the day is power you don't buy, and the surplus goes back to the grid against your bill.

[Explanation / Example] Here is how it worked for [named household, city, with consent]. Their summer bill was [₹ before]. They installed a [x kW] system through a vendor on the scheme's list, got [₹ subsidy amount under the current notice] back in their account [x weeks] after inspection, and their bill for the same month the next year was [₹ after]. The paperwork took one visit to the discom office and a few uploads from a phone. The vendor filed most of it.

[Opinion] So the subsidy is not the reason to go solar; your roof is. The subsidy is the reason to do it now, while the scheme is open and vendors in your district have a queue you can still join. Check two things this week: your sanctioned load on the last bill, and the list of registered vendors for your discom. Then ask two of them for a site visit.

samples.brief: framework fw:pas for topic: a 30-day English-speaking course for Tier-2 college students; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Problem > Agitate > Solution), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
[Problem] Campus placement ka GD round. Topic mil gaya, points dimaag mein ready hain, par English mein pehla sentence bolte hi atak gaye. Baaki log bol rahe hain, aur aap sirf sun rahe ho, apni baari ka wait karte hue jo kabhi aati nahi.

[Agitate] Yeh sirf GD mein nahi hota. Viva mein, internship ke phone call pe, HR round mein bhi. Answer aapko pata hota hai, par shortlist usko milti hai jo pehle aur saaf bolta hai. Aur har baar chup rehne se agli baar bolna aur mushkil lagta hai.

[Solution] BolChaal 30 isi ek cheez pe kaam karta hai: bolna. Roz shaam 7 baje 40 minute ka live session, 6 students ka group, aur rule simple hai: har student har din kam se kam teen baar bolega, sirf sunega nahi. Topics wahi jo aapke saamne aayenge: self-introduction, GD, "tell me about yourself", phone pe HR. Day 1 pe aap 2 minute ki recording bhejte ho, Day 30 pe wahi topic dobara. Dono recordings aap khud sun ke decide karte ho ki farak pada ya nahi. [past student's Day 1 vs Day 30 clip, shared with consent]. Fees ₹1,999 poore 30 din ki, hostel ke phone se join kar sakte ho. Agla batch 1 November se. Pehli class free hai: bio mein link pe naam aur college daalo, aur aaj shaam ke session mein aa jao.

samples.brief: framework fw:pastor for topic: a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Problem > Amplify > Story > Transformation > Offer > Response), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
[Problem] You run finance at a mid-size company, and month-end still means one analyst, two monitors and an Excel sheet matching bank credits to invoices, UTR by UTR.

[Amplify] Unmatched receipts sit in suspense. Collections chases customers who have already paid, and one of them says so to your CEO. The close slips past the 10th, and your best analyst spends a week a month matching numbers instead of reading them. She notices, and so does her LinkedIn.

[Story] Our co-founder was that analyst at a Bengaluru logistics firm. Every month-end she matched payments that came with half a customer name and no invoice number. Then she wrote a script that matched on amount, date and UTR, and sent only the leftovers to a human. That script became Reconcly.

[Transformation] Teams on Reconcly stop maintaining the matching sheet. The analyst clears an exceptions queue, and the ledger in Tally or Zoho Books updates itself. [Customer result: name, role, company, close date before and after, with written consent].

[Offer] Bank feeds, two-way Tally or Zoho Books sync, the exceptions queue, and our team setting up your matching rules in week one. ₹24,000 a month per legal entity. Start with a 30-day pilot on last quarter's data; if the matched file isn't useful, you pay nothing.

[Response] 1. Reply "pilot" to this email. 2. Fill in the read-only access form we send for one bank account. 3. Upload last quarter's invoices. Within a week, the matched file is in your inbox.

samples.brief: framework fw:pixar_story_spine for topic: a monsoon skincare range from an Ayurvedic D2C brand; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Once upon a time > Every day > But one day > Because of that (x3) > Until finally > And ever since then), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
[Once upon a time] there was a vaidya's granddaughter in Kochi named Meera, who sold skincare made from her grandmother's handwritten recipes.

[Every day] she packed the same jars: a rich kumkumadi cream and a besan ubtan. They sold well from October to March, and every year sales went quiet when the rains came. She blamed the season.

[But one day] in July, a customer from Mumbai wrote to her: "Your cream feels like wearing ghee in a local train." She had stopped using it.

[Because of that] Meera went back to her grandmother's notebook and found a page she had skipped for years, on varsha ritu: lighter oils, bitter herbs, less on the skin when the air is already wet.

[Because of that] she rebuilt the routine for the rains: a water-light neem and vetiver gel, a clay wash, and a face oil used three drops at a time.

[Because of that] she needed proof in real humidity, not in her air-conditioned unit, so she sent trial jars to customers in Mumbai, Kochi and Guwahati and asked each for one honest note at the end of every wet week.

[Until finally] the notes came back without the word "sticky", and the monsoon range went on sale in June, before the first rain.

[And ever since then] the shelf changes twice a year, rich for winter and light for the rains, and every June the first box goes to the woman in Mumbai who complained.

Appeal from the Rampur Tola road group to the next village, read out at the chaupal and shared on WhatsApp.

[Picture] Socho, saawan ki subah. Bitiya cycle se school nikal rahi hai aur pahiya kichad mein nahi phans raha. Doodh ki gaadi darwaze tak aa rahi hai. Raat ko kisi ki tabiyat bigde, toh tempo seedha ghar ke aage ruk sakta hai, kisi ko kandhe pe utha ke mod tak nahi le jaana padta.

[Promise] Hamare gaon ne yeh kaam ek WhatsApp group se kiya, aur aapka tola bhi kar sakta hai. Hum aapko poora tareeka denge: group kaise banta hai, chanda ka hisaab har hafte group mein kaise daalte hain, eent aur gitti ka rate kaise milate hain, aur shramdaan ki baari kaise lagti hai taaki kisi ek pe bojh na pade.

[Prove] Hamari sadak ki pehle aur baad ki photo group mein hai, aaj bhi dekh sakte ho. [Road length, total cost and per-household share from the group's ledger]. Har rupaye ki parchi group mein post hui thi, aur [mukhiya or ward member, name, on record] ne kaam khud dekha hai.

[Push] Kaam barsaat se pehle hi ho sakta hai, kyunki geeli mitti pe eent nahi baithti. Is Ravivar shaam 5 baje panchayat bhawan aao. Sirf ek kaam karna hai: apne tole se do log bhejo, jo hisaab rakhna jaante hon. Baaki hum dikha denge.

samples.brief: framework fw:prep for topic: a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C brands; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Point > Reason > Example > Point), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Question from a founder at our Jaipur D2C meetup: "Got an ASMT-10 for a GSTR-1 mismatch. Can my accounts person just reply?"

[Point] Let your accounts person collect the data, but let a CA draft and file the reply.

[Reason] The first reply is not a formality. It goes on record, and if the officer isn't satisfied with it, that same reply becomes the starting point for a demand notice. What you say first, you will be defending later.

[Example] Take the mismatch D2C brands see most often: your GSTR-1 shows one figure, and the marketplace's TCS return shows another for the same months. The usual cause is ordinary: returns and cancellations the marketplace booked in a different month from you, or orders shipped from a warehouse registered in another state. The fix is a reconciliation sheet, order by order, with the marketplace's settlement reports attached and a short covering letter that explains each gap. A reply that says "we are checking and will revert" explains nothing, and the officer is entitled to move ahead without you. [client case: notice type, what the self-filed reply said, how it was resolved].

[Point] So here is the split I'd suggest. Your team downloads the marketplace settlement reports and your sales register for the months in the notice, today. You send us those files with the notice PDF on WhatsApp. We send you a draft reply to review before it goes on the portal, well inside the deadline printed on the notice.

samples.brief: framework fw:problem_promise_proof_proposal for topic: a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Problem > Promise > Proof > Proposal), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
To: Admin and HR lead, [IT services company], Hinjewadi Phase 2
Subject: Office lunch your fitness programme can stand behind

[Problem] Your wellness programme tells employees to eat more protein, and the cafeteria thali gives them rice, aloo and a thin dal. So the people who care order outside: separate deliveries at the gate every afternoon, food that arrives cold, and a lunch break that runs long while they wait.

[Promise] ProtiThali will deliver a vegetarian high-protein thali to your floor by 12:45 every working day, with [protein per thali, lab-tested] in every box and the menu rotating weekly so nobody eats the same dal twice in a week. If a box reaches you after 1:00, that box is free.

[Proof] The protein figure comes from [accredited lab, report dated], and we will retest every quarter and share the report with your team. We already deliver daily lunches to [comparable Pune office: name, headcount, with permission], and their admin lead, [name], has agreed to take your call. You can also taste it first, at your desk, before signing anything.

[Proposal] ₹189 per thali for a minimum of 40 thalis a day, invoiced monthly with GST, no lock-in beyond 30 days' notice. We will start with one free tasting lunch for 20 people from your wellness group. Can we bring it to your office on Thursday at 1 pm?

samples.brief: framework fw:quest for topic: an AI tool that turns Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Qualify > Understand > Educate > Stimulate > Transition), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
[Qualify] Yeh un business owners ke liye hai jinki team ki meetings WhatsApp voice notes pe chalti hain, zyaadatar Hindi mein. Agar aapki meetings Zoom pe English mein hoti hain aur koi already minutes likhta hai, toh yahin ruk jaiye. Aapko iski zaroorat nahi.

[Understand] Aapka din kuch aisa hai: subah 8 baje supervisor ka 5 minute ka voice note, phir accountant ka, phir vendor ka. Shaam tak bees notes. Aur jab koi poochhta hai, "Woh delivery date kya fix hui thi?", toh aap scroll karke dobara sunte ho. Likhne ka time kisi ke paas nahi hota.

[Educate] Dikkat voice note mein nahi hai. Dikkat yeh hai ki decisions audio mein band ho jaate hain, jahan unhe koi search nahi kar sakta. Isliye fix ko teen kaam karne chahiye: Hindi aur Hinglish samajhna; poora transcript nahi, sirf decision, kaam kiska hai aur date alag nikaalna; aur WhatsApp pe hi chalna, kyunki team naya app nahi seekhegi. BoloMinutes yahi teen kaam karta hai.

[Stimulate] Socho, Monday ki review meeting. Pichhle hafte ke saare decisions ek page pe hain, naam aur date ke saath. Koi "maine toh aisa nahi bola tha" nahi. [beta user quote: name, business, city, with consent].

[Transition] Pehle 30 din free, phir ₹499 mahina poori team ke liye. Pasand na aaye toh cancel karne ka jhanjhat nahi, bas forward karna band kar do. Abhi apna koi purana voice note [WhatsApp number] pe forward karo aur khud dekho minutes kaise dikhte hain.

samples.brief: framework fw:reason_why_copy for topic: a government scheme that gives rooftop-solar subsidies to households; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Research the product > Find the untold reason > State it with specifics > Prove and test), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Campaign copy for the rooftop-solar subsidy scheme.

[Research the product] We read the scheme guidelines end to end, spent a day on inspection visits with a discom junior engineer in [district], and asked registered vendors what households ask them first. The answer was always the same: "Paisa milega ya nahi, aur panel chalega ya nahi?" Every ad answers the first half. None answers the second.

[Find the untold reason] Every subsidised system is inspected by the discom before the subsidy is released [confirm wording against the current guidelines]. Every system goes through it, so nobody mentions it. Yet it answers the fear that stops people: a government engineer checks the panels, inverter, wiring and net meter before a single rupee of subsidy is paid.

[State it with specifics] Headline: "Aapki chhat ke panel sarkari engineer check karega. Uske baad subsidy aayegi." Body: Because the subsidy is released only after the discom inspection, a vendor who cuts corners does not get paid by the scheme. The engineer checks [inspection items listed in the guidelines]. Then the money goes into your bank account, not the vendor's.

[Prove and test] Offer: a free bill check on WhatsApp. Send your last electricity bill and a roof photo; we reply with the system size that fits your load. Test: for two weeks, run headline A ("Subsidy seedha aapke khaate mein") against headline B (the inspection line) on the district broadcast lists, and keep whichever brings more completed portal registrations.

samples.brief: framework fw:rogerian_argument for topic: a 30-day English-speaking course for Tier-2 college students; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Introduce and show understanding > Where they are right > Your position > How they gain), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Note to the TPO and English department, [college], before Friday's staff meeting.

[Introduce and show understanding] Several of you have said we should not bring a 30-day English-speaking course onto campus. Your view, as I understand it: language takes years, short courses sell fluency they cannot deliver, and our students' money and time are better spent on the syllabus and on reading. If I have that wrong, please correct me on Friday.

[Where they are right] On fluency, you are right. Nobody's grammar, vocabulary or accent changes in a month, and any course that promises "fluent English in 30 days" is overselling. Students who need to rebuild basic grammar need a semester, not a sprint.

[Your position] My point is narrower. Most of our final-years have studied English for twelve years. What stops them in a GD or an HR round is not grammar. It is the first sentence. They have never had to speak English out loud, every day, in front of peers. A 30-day course built only on daily speaking can break that hesitation before placement season.

[How they gain] So here is a proposal we could both sign. Run one 30-day speaking batch for final-years in November, with no fluency claims in any notice. Record each student on Day 1 and Day 30 on the same topic, and let the English department judge the recordings. If the department doesn't hear a difference, we stop. If it does, the department designs the next batch.

samples.brief: framework fw:save_the_cat for topic: a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Opening Image > Theme Stated > Set-up > Catalyst > Debate > Break into Two > B Story > Fun and Games > Midpoint > Bad Guys Close In > All Is Lost > Dark Night of the Soul > Break into Three > Finale > Final Image), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Three-minute Reconcly brand film.

[Opening Image] 11 pm, Whitefield. Kavya alone in a dark finance bay, an Excel sheet glowing red.

[Theme Stated] The cleaner, switching off lights: "Madam, roz ka hisaab roz karo, toh raat nahi hoti."

[Set-up] Kavya takes a colleague's accounts so he can sit with his sick mother. Close: Friday. Her sister's engagement: Saturday.

[Catalyst] The CFO: auditors arrive Monday, not next month.

[Debate] IT suggests a reconciliation tool. Kavya refuses: "Machine galat match karegi, blame mera."

[Break into Two] She uploads one bank account to Reconcly, to prove it wrong.

[B Story] Papa calls nightly: "Khaana khaaya?" She always says yes.

[Fun and Games] Rows turn green in batches. A two-rupee rounding gap, flagged. A UPI credit from "BHAIYA KIRANA" makes her laugh.

[Midpoint] By Wednesday most of the month matches. She thinks she's done.

[Bad Guys Close In] A second bank account. A client paying three invoices in one transfer. The CFO wants a draft Thursday.

[All Is Lost] Her wrong rule matched a payment to the wrong customer. The CFO doubts the whole file.

[Dark Night of the Soul] On the office stairs, engagement photos buzzing, she lets Papa's call ring out.

[Break into Three] She calls back. Papa, thirty years a shopkeeper: "Ek niyam, ek hafta, haath se check."

[Finale] She rebuilds rules one at a time, checks every exception herself, closes Friday at six.

[Final Image] Saturday night. Dark office, every row green. Kavya dancing at the engagement, phone face down.

samples.brief: framework fw:schwartz_awareness_levels for topic: a monsoon skincare range from an Ayurvedic D2C brand; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Most aware > Product-aware > Solution-aware > Problem-aware > Unaware), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Barkha monsoon range, Ayurvedic skincare: five openings, one per awareness level.

[Most aware] Barkha Monsoon Kit (neem-vetiver gel, multani clay wash, face oil): ₹899 till Sunday, ₹1,099 from Monday when the launch price ends. Free shipping. Order today; it reaches you before the next spell of rain.

[Product-aware] Know Barkha but wondering if it's just our winter cream in a new jar? It isn't. The gel has no heavy oils, the clay wash replaces your foaming face wash for these months, and the oil is three drops at night. "Will it dry me out?" That's what the oil is for. [Review from a Mumbai customer, name and city, with consent].

[Solution-aware] You want skin that doesn't feel wrapped in cling film by noon in July. That takes a lighter routine: a gel instead of cream, a gentle clay wash, a few drops of oil. Barkha puts all three in one kit, built on Ayurveda's varsha ritu recipes for the rains.

[Problem-aware] Sticky by 11 am, small breakouts along the jawline, and a moisturiser that feels like ghee in this humidity? Your winter routine is too heavy for the rains. Monsoon skin needs less, and lighter.

[Unaware] "Mumbai local mein meri cream pighal jaati hai." A customer wrote that to us last July. Ayurveda has a name for this season, varsha ritu, and an old rule for it: when the air is wet, put less on your skin. That rule became our monsoon kit.

samples.brief: framework fw:scqa for topic: a Bihar civic story: a village that fixed its own road with a WhatsApp group; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Situation > Complication > Question > Answer), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Note to the DM from the BDO, [block]: citizen-funded road repairs.

[Situation] Link roads in this block get repaired one way: the mukhiya raises the request, the block forwards it, and the road waits for the next sanction.

[Complication] In [village], the link road to the main road broke in last year's rains. The villagers did not wait. A WhatsApp group of [number] households pooled money, bought brick and gitti at rates they compared in the group, did the labour as shramdaan, and posted every receipt there. The road is usable today. Now three nearby villages want to copy it, and we have no rule for residents repairing a public road with their own money.

[Question] Should the block back these WhatsApp repairs, and if so, how do we do it without losing control of quality and accounts?

[Answer] Yes. Back them, under a one-page protocol. Three points support this.
First, quality: a junior engineer signs off on the material and thickness before work starts and inspects once after, so a weak repair doesn't become our problem next monsoon.
Second, accounts: the group's ledger and receipts are read out at the gram sabha, which keeps the money with the people who paid it and keeps us out of handling it.
Third, fairness: a village that repairs its own road stays on the government repair list. Otherwise we punish the villages that helped themselves. We request approval to pilot this in the three villages before December.

samples.brief: framework fw:shorts_loop for topic: a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C brands; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Pick the seam > Write the opening as the second half > Body > Write the ending as the first half > Match picture and sound), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Hinglish Short, Jaipur CA firm, GST notices for D2C founders.

[Pick the seam] Seam sentence: "Aur sabse badi galti yeh maan lena hai ki / GST notice khud expire ho jaata hai. Nahi hota." The last line carries the first half; the opening carries the second.

[Write the opening as the second half] "...GST notice khud expire ho jaata hai. Nahi hota."

[Body] "Notice aaye toh usi din teen kaam. Ek: portal se notice PDF download karo aur reply ki last date apne calendar mein daalo, phone pe alarm ke saath. Do: jin mahino ka notice hai, unka GSTR-1 aur marketplace ka settlement report nikaalo. Zyaadatar mismatch yahin dikh jaata hai: returns, cancellations, ya doosre state ka warehouse. Teen: har farak ki order-wise sheet banao aur reply ke saath lagao. Reply mein 'we are checking and will revert' kabhi mat likhna. Woh kuch explain nahi karta, aur officer aage badh sakta hai."

[Write the ending as the first half] "Aur sabse badi galti yeh maan lena hai ki..." (cut straight to the opening line, nothing after it)

[Match picture and sound] Same mid-shot at both ends: CA at the desk, laptop open on the GST portal, hand on the same file. Ceiling-fan hum runs under the whole reel, so the cut has no audio jump. No "follow for more" at the end. The ask goes in the caption: "Notice aaya hai? Photo WhatsApp karo, link bio mein."

samples.brief: framework fw:skyscraper_technique for topic: a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Find link-worthy content > Make something clearly better > Reach out), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Link-building plan: ProtiThali, Pune cloud kitchen, high-protein veg thali launch.

[Find link-worthy content] In [backlink tool], check who ranks and gets linked for "high protein vegetarian diet India" and "protein in Indian food". Pick the page with the most relevant referring domains: gym blogs, diabetes forums, college hostel groups. [URL of the top page, its referring-domain count and publish date, from the tool]. Pages like this are usually a table of protein per 100 g of raw ingredients. That doesn't tell anyone what's in an actual plate of dal-chawal.

[Make something clearly better] Publish "How much protein is in a real Maharashtrian veg lunch?" with what the original lacks: lab-tested protein for cooked dishes as served, from varan-bhaat to usal to paneer bhurji [lab report, dated]; cost per 10 g of protein across common Pune options at current prices [prices checked, with date]; a printable one-week veg lunch plan; a Marathi edition; and a Pune dietitian [name] answering the five questions customers send us most on WhatsApp. ProtiThali appears once, as one row in the cost table, tested by the same lab method.

[Reach out] From the linking list, keep only sites whose readers would use this, likely gyms, hostel and PG pages, and diabetes support groups. Write to each person by name, one at a time: "Your protein-for-vegetarians page links to [original]. Ours has lab numbers for cooked Maharashtrian dishes and a Marathi version, if that helps your members." No bulk templates; one follow-up at most.

[Stop] Boss ne 7 minute ka Hindi voice note bheja hai. Aur aapko bas yeh jaanna hai ki aapko kya karna hai.

samples.brief: framework fw:star for topic: a government scheme that gives rooftop-solar subsidies to households; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Situation > Task > Action > Result), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Interview question: "Tell me about a time you got people to act on something they were hesitant about."

[Situation] In 2025 I was the field coordinator for a rooftop-solar vendor in [Tier-2 city], registered under the household subsidy scheme. Enquiries came in steadily, but most families dropped out before submitting the subsidy application.

[Task] I owned that gap. My target was to convert [number] stalled enquiries into completed applications before the quarter closed, without adding sales staff.

[Action] First I called the families who had dropped out and asked one question: where did you stop? Almost every answer was the portal, not the price: the login, finding the consumer number on the bill, uploading documents from a phone. So I set up a Saturday help desk in two RWA offices with a laptop and a printer, and wrote a one-page Hindi checklist: last bill, bank passbook, roof photo. The key decision was who staffed it. I pulled our sales executives and sent our installation engineer instead, because families trusted the person who would actually climb their roof. I also called every family the day their subsidy was credited and asked them to tell one neighbour.

[Result] [Applications completed in the quarter, against the previous quarter]; [households with subsidy credited by quarter-end]. What I took from it: when people hesitate, it's usually the paperwork, not the idea. I now start every outreach by asking where people stopped.

samples.brief: framework fw:star_story_solution for topic: a 30-day English-speaking course for Tier-2 college students; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Star > Story > Solution), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Reel script for BolChaal 30. Draft for a real student story: replace every detail with the student's own account, used with her written consent.

[Star] Pooja, final-year BCom at a college in Sagar. First in her family to sit a campus placement.

[Story] She cleared the aptitude test for a bank's back-office job. Then came the group discussion. Points ready, notebook full, but the first English sentence wouldn't come out, and the round ended before she spoke once. That night she watched YouTube speaking videos till 1 am and practised lines in front of the hostel mirror. The mirror never answered back. The next drive was six weeks away, and her father had already told the whole mohalla about the first one.

[Solution] A senior sent her the BolChaal 30 link. Every evening at 7: forty minutes, a group of six, and one rule, every student speaks at least three times. On Day 1 she recorded two minutes on "tell me about yourself", and her voice shook. On Day 30 she recorded the same topic and sent both clips to her father. [Her result at the next drive, in her own words, with consent].

Your next drive has a date too. Agla batch 1 November se shuru. Pehli class free hai: bio mein link pe apna naam aur college daalo, aur aaj shaam 7 baje join karo.

samples.brief: framework fw:storybrand_sb7 for topic: a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation; 150-250 words following the steps in order (A character > Has a problem > Meets a guide > Who gives them a plan > And calls them to action > That helps them avoid failure > And ends in a success), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Homepage message map for Reconcly, a Bengaluru invoice-reconciliation SaaS. Each part becomes a page section.

[A character] You run finance for a growing company, and you want one thing from month-end: books closed by the 5th that you can sign without a knot in your stomach.

[Has a problem] But bank credits arrive with half a customer name and no invoice number. Someone matches them by hand in Excel, the close drifts to the 10th, and when the CFO asks "are we closed?", you say yes while knowing the suspense account says otherwise.

[Meets a guide] We know that sheet. Our co-founder spent years matching UTRs by hand in a Bengaluru finance team before she built Reconcly. It speaks Tally and Zoho Books, and it understands the customer who pays three invoices in one transfer. [Customer count and named logos, with permission].

[Who gives them a plan] 1. Connect your bank accounts and your books, read-only. 2. We set up your matching rules with your team in week one. 3. Your analyst clears only the exceptions.

[And calls them to action] Button: "Start a 30-day pilot on last quarter's data."

[That helps them avoid failure] Without it, the next close slips again, collections chases customers who already paid, and the auditor's first query is about your suspense entries.

[And ends in a success] Next quarter: closed by the 5th, every credit tied to an invoice, and your analyst spending month-end reading the numbers instead of matching them.

samples.brief: framework fw:thread_structure for topic: a monsoon skincare range from an Ayurvedic D2C brand; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Hook post > Context (optional) > Body posts > Summary > CTA), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
X thread from the founder of an Ayurvedic skincare brand, launching its monsoon range.

[Hook post] Our winter cream stops selling every July. It took us three monsoons to understand why. Here are the 5 changes we now make to skincare when the rains start, straight from my grandmother's vaidya notebook:

[Context (optional)] Ayurveda treats the rains, varsha ritu, as a season of their own, with one rule for skin that I ignored for years: when the air is wet, put less on it.

[Body posts]
1/5 Swap cream for gel. In humid weather a heavy cream just sits on top, and by noon it feels like a layer of ghee.

2/5 Wash with clay, not foam. A clay wash lifts sweat and city grime without the tight, stripped feeling that sends you back to the cream jar.

3/5 Oil goes on at night, three drops. Not zero: skin still loses water all day under the fan and the office AC.

4/5 Dry your face properly after you get caught in the rain. Damp skin under a helmet or dupatta for hours is asking for trouble.

5/5 Keep the sunscreen. Grey skies still let UV through, and July tans are real.

[Summary] Monsoon skin, in one line: gel over cream, clay over foam, three drops of oil at night, a dry face, sunscreen anyway.

[CTA] If someone you know is still using winter cream in July, repost the first post for them.

samples.brief: framework fw:three_act_structure for topic: a Bihar civic story: a village that fixed its own road with a WhatsApp group; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Act 1: Setup > Act 2: Confrontation > Act 3: Resolution), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Two-minute civic-campaign film, Bihar, drawn from a village that fixed its road through WhatsApp.

[Act 1: Setup] Monsoon, a tola outside Darbhanga. Rakesh, 24, is home after losing his Delhi job. One night his neighbour Kamla chachi collapses. The ambulance stops at the main road; the link road is knee-deep slush. Four men carry her a kilometre on a khatiya. Next morning he asks: "Agli barsaat se pehle yeh sadak kaun banayega?"

[Act 2: Confrontation] He starts a WhatsApp group, "Hamari Sadak". Eleven people join, then stop replying. At the chai shop, someone says it aloud: "Chanda le ke Dilli bhaag jaayega." So Rakesh posts every receipt in the group. The group grows. The brick supplier quotes high; Rakesh posts three rates side by side and the supplier comes down. Then the first stretch they lay washes out in one storm. Half the group goes silent again. In the next village, retired mistri Ramji shows him that a road dies from the water under it.

[Act 3: Resolution] The second rains are a week away and the last stretch, outside Kamla chachi's house, is still mud. Rakesh posts one message: "Aaj raat, torch le ke aaiye." The whole tola comes. The mukhiya, who had said "sanction ka intezaar karo", sends the panchayat tractor. By dawn the last stretch is laid, drain first, the way Ramji showed. In the final shot, ambulance headlights pull up right at a doorway, and Kamla chachi waves them off: it's for someone else this time.

samples.brief: framework fw:topic_cluster for topic: a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C brands; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Choose the pillar topic > Map the cluster > Write the pillar page > Write the cluster pages > Maintain), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Content plan: Jaipur CA firm, GST notices for D2C brands.

[Choose the pillar topic] GST notices for D2C and marketplace sellers. Founders search it the week a notice lands, and we handle these daily, so we write with authority.

[Map the cluster] From client WhatsApps and calls, one page per intent: what an ASMT-10 is and how to reply; why GSTR-1 doesn't match the marketplace's TCS figures; ITC mismatch notices between GSTR-3B and 2B; what happens after a DRC-01; finding portal notices nobody emailed you; notices for an out-of-state warehouse.

[Write the pillar page] "GST notices for D2C brands: what each one means and what to do this week". It answers the broad question on its own, one section per subtopic, each linking to its cluster page with a descriptive anchor: "how to reply to an ASMT-10 scrutiny notice".

[Write the cluster pages] Each page goes deep on one question, with a worked example, documents to collect and the reply structure we use. Each links back with "every GST notice type for D2C sellers" and to a sibling where it helps: the ASMT-10 page links to "what happens if your scrutiny reply is not accepted".

[Maintain] Every month, new client questions become new cluster pages, written by the CA who handled them, never batch-generated. Refresh the pillar when forms or rules change, with the date on top. Each quarter, crawl for orphan and broken links. Pitch it to partners as a planning discipline, never a ranking promise.

samples.brief: framework fw:toulmin_model for topic: a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Claim > Grounds > Warrant > Backing > Qualifier > Rebuttal), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Note to the ProtiThali founders before launch.

[Claim] We should print the lab-tested protein figure on every thali box from day one, not the figure from our recipe calculator.

[Grounds] The recipe calculator and the lab report give different numbers for the same thali [both figures, from the lab report dated ___]. In the pre-launch tasting, the first question on almost every feedback card was "how much protein is actually in this?" Our customers are gym regulars and people tracking their diet, often in an app.

[Warrant] People who buy a high-protein meal are buying the number. If the number on the box is wrong, they stop trusting the meal, however good it tastes.

[Backing] Any packaged food brand making a nutrition claim has to be able to substantiate it [FSSAI labelling and claims rules: confirm with our food-safety consultant how they apply to cloud-kitchen meals]. Fitness customers also compare notes publicly, so a figure that doesn't hold up gets found out in reviews.

[Qualifier] In most weeks, a lab test each quarter should keep the printed figure close to what is in the box, provided the kitchen keeps weighing paneer and dal for every portion as it does now.

[Rebuttal] The exception is new dishes. If the menu rotates faster than we can test, we print a protein range per thali type rather than one exact number, and no dish goes on the label until it has been through the lab once.

samples.brief: framework fw:usp for topic: an AI tool that turns Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes; 150-250 words following the steps in order (List what you do better > Strike shared claims > Pick one proposition > Say it in one line, everywhere), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Working note: the USP for BoloMinutes (Hindi voice notes to meeting minutes).

[List what you do better] For a small-business owner whose team talks in WhatsApp voice notes: it understands Hindi and Hinglish in the same note; it works inside WhatsApp, with no app to install; it returns decisions, owners and dates as separate lines, not a wall of transcript; it replies in Hindi or English; it costs ₹299 a month; it deletes the audio after processing [confirm with engineering].

[Strike shared claims] Hindi transcription: several tools already claim it. "AI meeting notes": every video-call tool says this, and so do we, so it goes. Low price: anyone can undercut us next quarter. Privacy: everyone claims it, and nobody can check it. What's left: it works on forwarded WhatsApp voice notes and sends back who does what by when, in the same chat [verify against the three nearest competitors, with date].

[Pick one proposition] Forward any Hindi voice note on WhatsApp and get back who does what, by when, in the same chat. A site or shop owner feels it on day one, and we can demonstrate it live in a sales call.

[Say it in one line, everywhere] "Voice note bhejo. Kaam ki list pao." It goes on the WhatsApp business profile, the first frame of every ad, the website headline, the footer of every minutes PDF, and it's the first sentence every salesperson says. The supporting points stay in the second line, never in the first.

samples.brief: framework fw:what_so_what_now_what for topic: a government scheme that gives rooftop-solar subsidies to households; 150-250 words following the steps in order (What? > So what? > Now what?), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
September update from the solar committee of [housing society] to residents and the managing committee, on the rooftop-solar subsidy scheme.

[What?] We ran two Saturday help desks in the clubhouse. [Number] households came; [number] submitted subsidy applications on the portal; [number] have had their system installed and inspected. [Number] applications are waiting for the discom's feasibility approval, the oldest since [date]. Two families stopped because their roof is shared with a water tank and the vendor could not fit enough panels.

[So what?] Interest is not the problem, and neither is the money. The queue is at one step: discom feasibility. Applications that cleared it moved to installation quickly. The help desk works for families who come, but towers C and D sent almost nobody, and those are mostly elderly residents who may not use the portal. Shared roofs also need a society-level answer, not a household one.

[Now what?] Mr [name], committee secretary, will take the list of pending applications to the discom assistant engineer by 15 October and report back in the group. Ms [name] will run a door-to-door help session in towers C and D on 19 October, with the vendor's engineer present. The managing committee will discuss using the common terrace for families with shared roofs at the 2 November meeting; we need a yes or no on putting it on the agenda by 25 October.

samples.brief: framework fw:writers_journey_vogler for topic: a 30-day English-speaking course for Tier-2 college students; 150-250 words following the steps in order (The Ordinary World > The Call to Adventure > Refusal of the Call > Meeting with the Mentor > Crossing the First Threshold > Tests, Allies, and Enemies > Approach to the Innermost Cave > The Ordeal > Reward > The Road Back > The Resurrection > Return with the Elixir), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
Three-minute brand film for BolChaal 30. The student is the hero; the course is the mentor.

[The Ordinary World] Sameer, final-year BSc, Bareilly. Tops every written exam. In English, he answers only in his head.

[The Call to Adventure] An IT company announces a campus drive, with a communication round.

[Refusal of the Call] He skips the pre-placement talk. "Meri English ka mazaak banega."

[Meeting with the Mentor] A senior sends him the BolChaal 30 link. Trainer Naina's first rule: "Galat bolo, par bolo."

[Crossing the First Threshold] Day 1: he records two shaky minutes on his phone and presses send.

[Tests, Allies, and Enemies] In his group of six, a girl from Budaun becomes his practice partner. His roommate mimics his accent every night.

[Approach to the Innermost Cave] Day 25: a mock HR round, with Naina playing the interviewer.

[The Ordeal] "Tell me about yourself." He blanks and logs off mid-round.

[Reward] Naina sends him two clips: Day 1, and the first minute of the mock before he froze. He hears the difference himself.

[The Road Back] Two days to the drive. The roommate's jokes, and his father asking on the phone, "Taiyaari ho gayi?"

[The Resurrection] The real panel asks something he never practised. He answers in plain English, pausing, and doesn't stop.

[Return with the Elixir] Sunday evening, hostel corridor: Sameer runs a speaking circle for juniors, with Naina's rule taped to the door.

samples.brief: framework fw:youtube_intro_hook_promise_preview for topic: a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation; 150-250 words following the steps in order (Hook > Promise > Preview > Deliver), each step labelled in square brackets
samples.text:
YouTube intro, Reconcly channel. Title: "Match unidentified bank credits to invoices in Excel". Thumbnail: a bank line, "NEFT RAJ ENTERP ₹47,200", with a question mark.

[Hook] This bank credit says "NEFT RAJ ENTERP, ₹47,200". No invoice number, and you have four customers whose names start with Raj. Somebody in your team will spend the next twenty minutes on this one line. Now think about every line like it in your month.

[Promise] By the end of this video, you'll have a matching sheet in plain Excel that clears the easy matches on its own and leaves your analyst a short list of the ones that genuinely need a human.

[Preview] Three rules, in this order. First, match on UTR wherever the customer's payment advice gives you one. Second, amount plus a date window, for everything else. Third, the name match, which is where most sheets go wrong, and I'll show you the one formula that fixes it. I run finance operations at Reconcly, so I see this problem in [number of client bank statements] statements a month. And at the end, I'll show you the one kind of payment no rule should ever auto-match.

[Deliver] So open last month's bank statement export. Column A is the date, column B the narration, column C the credit amount. Now open your invoice register next to it. Step one: we pull the UTR out of the narration. Click on cell D2 and type this...
